Simulating trees with controlled shape

Source: vignettes/treeshapesim.Rmd
treeshapesim.Rmd
library(treeshapesim)
set.seed(1)

Two shape statistics, two processes

The gamma statistic of Pybus and Harvey (2000) summarizes the distribution of branching times: it is near zero for Yule trees and negative when branching times are concentrated near the root. The Colless index summarizes topological imbalance; normalized against its Yule expectation, it is near zero for Yule trees and positive for more imbalanced ones. tree_shape() returns both.

sim_tree_shape() draws the topology from Aldous’ beta-splitting model (beta) and the internode intervals from a pure-birth process in which each of the k lineages splits at rate k^c (c). The two are drawn independently, gamma depends only on the intervals and the Colless index only on the topology, so c moves gamma without changing the Colless index and beta does the opposite.

yule <- sim_tree_shape(100, nsim = 50)
early <- sim_tree_shape(100, c = -1, nsim = 50)
imbalanced <- sim_tree_shape(100, beta = -1.5, nsim = 50)
shapes <- lapply(list(yule = yule, early = early, imbalanced = imbalanced),
                 function(trees) colMeans(t(vapply(trees, tree_shape, numeric(2)))))
do.call(rbind, shapes)
#>                  gamma     colless
#> yule        0.31793823 -0.10063867
#> early      -5.58314659 -0.09283867
#> imbalanced  0.09541742 10.51216133

Reaching target values

The mean of each statistic depends on its parameter and on the number of tips. calibrate_shape() estimates both curves for a given number of tips, and shape_params() inverts them. Since each curve is estimated from its own process, without building trees, the calibration is fast. Use more draws per value (reps, 200 by default) for a study; a few are enough here.

cal <- calibrate_shape(100, reps = 50)
cal
#> Shape calibration for n = 100 tips (50 draws per value)
#>   mean gamma from -8.46 to 9.44 for c in [ -2 , 1 ]
#>   mean Colless from -1.79 to 34.4 for beta in [ -1.95 , 8 ]
shape_params(cal, gamma = -2, colless = 1)
#>   gamma colless       beta          c
#> 1    -2       1 -0.5449625 -0.2866907

The parameters give the target values on average, but single trees vary around them. sim_tree_target() keeps only trees whose statistics fall within a tolerance of the targets. Because topology and intervals are independent, it rejects them separately, which gives the same distribution of trees as rejecting whole trees, with a much higher acceptance rate.

trees <- sim_tree_target(100, gamma = -2, colless = 1, nsim = 20, tol = 0.25,
                         calibration = cal, root_age = 50)
summary(attr(trees, "shape"))
#>      gamma           colless      
#>  Min.   :-2.242   Min.   :0.8008  
#>  1st Qu.:-2.085   1st Qu.:1.0058  
#>  Median :-1.957   Median :1.0608  
#>  Mean   :-1.971   Mean   :1.0398  
#>  3rd Qu.:-1.827   3rd Qu.:1.1058  
#>  Max.   :-1.756   Max.   :1.2008
attr(trees, "acceptance")
#>  topology intervals 
#> 0.1538462 0.1739130

A grid of tree shapes

For simulation studies, shape_grid() crosses levels of both statistics. The levels can come, for instance, from quantiles of tree_shape() over empirical trees of a similar size; here they are set by hand.

grid <- shape_grid(100, gamma = c(-2, -1, 0), colless = c(0, 0.5, 1),
                   calibration = cal)
grid
#>   gamma colless        beta           c
#> 1    -2     0.0  0.03840196 -0.28669067
#> 2    -1     0.0  0.03840196 -0.14838659
#> 3     0     0.0  0.03840196 -0.01769295
#> 4    -2     0.5 -0.26393708 -0.28669067
#> 5    -1     0.5 -0.26393708 -0.14838659
#> 6     0     0.5 -0.26393708 -0.01769295
#> 7    -2     1.0 -0.54496255 -0.28669067
#> 8    -1     1.0 -0.54496255 -0.14838659
#> 9     0     1.0 -0.54496255 -0.01769295
cell <- grid[grid$gamma == -1 & grid$colless == 0.5, ]
cell_trees <- sim_tree_target(100, gamma = cell$gamma, colless = cell$colless,
                              nsim = 10, calibration = cal)

Placing an empirical tree on the same scale

fit_shape() estimates beta from the topology and c from the branching times by maximum likelihood (the beta-splitting model and the DDX model of the R package laser, with c = -x), and a parametric bootstrap with the package’s own generators gives percentile intervals. The estimate of beta is imprecise for balanced trees with few tips, and c describes the shape of the lineage-through-time curve, not its cause.

empirical <- sim_tree_shape(150, beta = -1, c = -0.7)   # stands in for a real tree
fit_shape(empirical, boot = 30)
#> Shape estimates for a tree with 150 tips
#>      estimate   2.5%  97.5%
#> beta   -1.200 -1.360 -0.835
#> c      -0.678 -0.856 -0.496
#> gamma = -7.5 | normalized Colless = 7.13

References

Aldous, D. (1996). Probability distributions on cladograms. In D. Aldous & R. Pemantle (Eds.), Random discrete structures (pp. 1–18). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-0719-1_1

Pybus, O. G., & Harvey, P. H. (2000). Testing macro-evolutionary models using incomplete molecular phylogenies. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 267, 2267–2272. https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2000.1278
